Tech stocks were lower Friday afternoon, with the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) falling 2.2% and the State Street SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF (XSD) down 2.4%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor index shed 2.1%.

In corporate news, CoreWeave (CRWV) shares were down past 11% after Bloomberg reported that co-founders Michael Intrator, Brian Venturo and Brannin McBee have sold $3.3 billion in company shares since its March 2025 initial public offering, including $2.4 billion in 2026.

SpaceX's (SPCX) Starshield service, which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and drone operations, was slowed after an order from inside the White House to the Defense Department, Reuters reported Friday, citing two US officials and one Western official. A senior US official told Reuters that President Donald Trump had not requested the slowdown. SpaceX shares were shedding 2.1%.

Amazon-backed (AMZN) Anthropic has reached out to New York City Comptroller Mark Levine after he sent a letter Wednesday urging the company to delay its initial public offering, Levine said Friday on Bloomberg TV. In the letter, addressed to CEO Dario Amodei, Levine asked the AI lab to pause the IPO until it fully addresses safety and governance concerns it has raised, according to the report. Amazon shares were falling 1.8%.

Varonis Systems (VRNS) agreed to be acquired by Thoma Bravo portfolio firm Proofpoint in an all-cash deal valued at about $6.3 billion, the companies said late Thursday. Shares rose 2.8%.

title: Amazon Is 11% Below Its High Heading Into Earnings on Oct. 29. Here's the 1 Number That Will Decide What Happens Next.
detail:
Amazon Is 11% Below Its High Heading Into Earnings on Oct. 29. Here's the 1 Number That Will Decide What Happens Next.
Leo Sun, The Motley Fool

AMZN
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Amazon's (NASDAQ: AMZN) stock closed at its all-time high of $284.02 per share on Aug. 3, 2026. Today, it trades at about $254. Let's see why it pulled back about 11% -- and how one number could drive it higher or lower when it posts its third-quarter earnings on Oct. 29.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

What's the number everyone will be watching?

Amazon is the world's largest e-commerce and cloud infrastructure company. It generates most of its revenue from its retail business, but most of its operating profits come from Amazon Web Services (AWS), the world's largest cloud infrastructure platform.

AWS already hosts tens of millions of websites and apps, making it the backbone of the internet. It also hosts Bedrock, a managed service that enables organizations to build their own AI apps, SageMaker, a platform for training custom AI models, and a wide range of customized AI APIs. To support the growth of that AI ecosystem, Amazon is producing its own AI accelerator chips. Anthropic, in which Amazon owns a major stake, is one of AWS' leading customers.

AWS' year-over-year revenue growth has accelerated significantly over the past year, and its 36.7% growth in the second quarter marked its strongest growth in 18 quarters.

The AI market's explosive expansion drove AWS' growth, and analysts expect the segment's revenue to grow 30%-35% year over year in the third quarter. If it exceeds that range and accelerates for another consecutive quarter, its stock could soar higher. But if it falls short of that range, its stock could stumble -- since it's allocating most of its projected capex of $220 billion this year toward the expansion of AWS' AI infrastructure.

Will Amazon be revalued as a high-growth AI stock?

From 2025 to 2028, analysts expect Amazon's revenue and EPS to grow at CAGRs of 15% and 25%, respectively. Its stock still looks reasonably valued at 24 times next year's earnings -- but it could command a higher valuation if it's revalued as a high-growth AI infrastructure stock.

That's why investors should keep a close eye on AWS' growth rates in the third quarter, and whether or not Amazon raises its capex guidance again to support that expansion. If it maintains its high growth rates without significantly boosting capex, its stock could reach new highs in the near future.

US benchmark equity indexes slid intraday as several major technology names sold off.

The Nasdaq Composite declined 1.9% to 26,199.2 intraday Friday, while the S&P 500 fell 1% to 7,664.2. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.5% to 51,928.6.

Among sectors, communication services and technology led the laggards, while energy paced the gainers.

Salesforce (CRM), Microsoft (MSFT), Cisco Systems (CSCO), Alphabet (GOOGL) and Amazon (AMZN) were the biggest decliners on the Dow.

Micron Technology (MU), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Sandisk (SNDK) were also falling.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite hit fresh closing highs Oct. 6, but the rally had been powered by only a few tech giants, suggesting underlying weakness on Wall Street.

Many analysts fear a potential stock market correction as the majority of S&P 500 stocks have been hovering well below all-time highs.

Treasury yields were higher intraday, with the two-year rate up 1.5 basis points at 4.77%, and the 10-year rate rising 2.3 basis points to 5.11%.

US industrial production grew more than expected in September as manufacturing output rebounded despite weakness in the auto component, Federal Reserve data showed.

Brent crude oil gained 3.1% to $109.24 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate increased 2.9% to $100.79.

Spot gold fell 0.3% to $4,158.46 per troy ounce, while silver increased 0.2% to $57.29 per ounce.

title: 2 Tech Stocks to Buy Now and Hold for a Decade (Hint: 1 Isn't in the AI Trade)
detail:
2 Tech Stocks to Buy Now and Hold for a Decade (Hint: 1 Isn't in the AI Trade)
Will Healy, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 8:37 AM MST 5 min read
AMZN
NVDA
SE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors understandably tie today's technology industry to artificial intelligence (AI). Since cutting-edge technology has driven much of the innovation, investors could easily fall into the trap of assuming that all tech companies are AI enterprises as well.

Nonetheless, in many tech enterprises, AI is more of a secondary growth driver. Given that, tech stocks like Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Sea Limited (NYSE: SE) should continue to drive long-term growth, even though only one is an AI company.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
The AI company: Amazon

Most of the public knows Amazon best for its e-commerce platform. This is crucial because no matter where one stands on the state of the market, the e-commerce part of the business is highly recession-resistant due to the wide variety of goods it offers.

However, even with faster-growth businesses like digital advertising and third-party seller services, its retail business is generally a slower-growth, lower-margin segment.

Instead, most of its growth comes from its AI-driven cloud arm, Amazon Web Services (AWS). Despite accounting for just 21% of the company's revenue in the first half of 2026, it delivers the majority of the company's operating income.

With that, Amazon reported $382 billion in net sales in the first two quarters of 2026, an 18% increase from the same period in 2025.

Admittedly, its net income points to struggles. Even though it reported $92 billion in profit in the first half of 2026, $69 billion came from investment gains. Thus, when subtracting those increases, Amazon's net income barely grew over the same period.

Other income also skewed its P/E ratio down to 21, an unusually low level for Amazon. Furthermore, after decades of reporting massive free cash flows, it reported a $7.6 billion outflow over the trailing 12 months. With the company pledging $220 billion in capital expenditures (capex), the cost of keeping up in the AI race has strained its balance sheet.

Nonetheless, its 31 forward P/E ratio suggests its valuation is well below historical levels. Additionally, the spending that has strained the balance sheet and income statement is an investment that should make the upside worth the risk. Thus, it likely pays to be patient with Amazon stock.

The non-AI company: Sea Limited

title: Does The Move In Snowflake Stock Change Anything?
detail:
Does The Move In Snowflake Stock Change Anything?
Trefis Team
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 8:54 AM MST 3 min read
SNOW
^GSPC
MSFT
AMZN
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pexels

Snowflake (SNOW) stock rose 59.3% from January 18 to October 15, 2026, against 12.5% for the S&P 500. The company reported quarterly results three times along the way, on February 25, May 27 and September 2. Buyers appear to be betting that customers using AI on Snowflake's data platform will keep its sales growth climbing while its losses shrink. So how much faster is Snowflake growing than it was in January?

Snowflake Has Grown Faster Every Quarter Since January

Snowflake's revenue is growing about five percentage points faster than when the rise began. Revenue grew 30.1% from a year earlier in fiscal Q4 2026, the quarter that ended January 31. That pace reached 35.1% in fiscal Q2 2027, with growth registering higher in each quarter along the way. Product revenue, nearly all of Snowflake's sales, grew 37% in that latest quarter. On the September 2 call, management said customers using AI on Snowflake consume more across the data platform.

The stock's two largest one-day gains during the rise came right after the May 27 and September 2 reports. Shares rose 37% on May 28, the day after Snowflake reported fiscal Q1 2027 results. On the September 2 call, management said it had raised its fiscal 2027 forecast for product revenue growth by more than five percentage points, to 36%. The stock gained 16.6% the next day.

A run higher can leave Snowflake a larger share of what you own than you planned. See how to protect a concentrated position.

How Far Have Snowflake's Losses Shrunk?

Snowflake's operating loss came to 17.0% of revenue in fiscal Q2 2027, against 29.7% in fiscal Q2 2026. The company's losses are narrowing, though it still loses money. Management said on the September 2 call that Snowflake remains on track for a profit under standard accounting rules (GAAP) in fiscal Q4 2028.

Yet management also said its fast-growing AI workloads carry a lower margin today. So Snowflake keeps less of each dollar on the sales that are lifting its growth, at least for now.

Why Snowflake Is Still Valued On Its Sales

Snowflake is still valued on its sales because it remains unprofitable, despite the faster growth. It lost $1.09 billion over the twelve months to July 31, 2026, so its price-to-earnings multiple is not meaningful. Its operating loss over those twelve months stood at 22.8% of revenue. That marks the smallest figure at any quarter end from fiscal Q2 2021 on, yet it is still a loss.

On sales, the stock trades at 21.5 times, against 3.1 for the S&P 500. At that multiple, the share price appears to assume that both the faster growth and the shrinking losses continue.
